source: US Army article citing FM 6-0 / ADP 5-0: Developing multiple sustainment COAs
finding: Doctrine places COA development as step 3 of the 7-step MDMP. A COA is a broad potential solution. Its purpose is to produce options for later analysis and comparison.
numbers: 7 steps: receipt of mission, mission analysis, COA development, COA analysis, COA comparison, COA approval, orders production.
quote: broad potential solution to an identified problem
limits: Secondary article, not the manual itself; year approximate. The 2022 FM 5-0 and JP 5-0 text was not opened.
agent_relevance: Our S3 'several distinct options' maps onto doctrine step 3. Doctrine is a prescription, not an evidence base.

source: US Army article citing FM 6-0: COA screening criteria
finding: Each COA is screened on five tests: feasible, acceptable, suitable, distinguishable, complete.
numbers: 5 criteria. Distinguishable means the COA must differ significantly from the other COAs.
quote: must differ significantly enough from other possible COAs
limits: Criteria are checklist items judged by staff. No measured validity for them was found in opened sources.
agent_relevance: Cheap code-checkable analogues: a distinctness test (diversity metric across candidates) and a completeness test (all required fields filled). Feasible, acceptable and suitable need a model or a simulator.

source: US Army article citing FM 6-0: number of COAs and the single-COA trend
finding: Doctrine wants two or more COAs in the best case. Under time pressure commanders may limit the number or tell the staff to work on one. The author reports planners presenting one COA, or COA teams returning near-identical plans.
numbers: Minimum: 2 or more in the best case. Exception: 1 under time limits. No counts given for the trend.
limits: Anecdote from one practitioner article about sustainment staffs.
agent_relevance: Warning for our agent: asking a model for N options can give N near-copies unless distinctness is enforced by code (G4: same-model samples are not independent).

source: Goecks & Waytowich (2024) COA-GPT: Generative Pre-trained Transformers for Accelerated Course of Action Development
finding: An LLM turns mission text, force lists (JSON) and doctrine excerpts into a structured COA: name, strategy text, one command per unit. A human can give text feedback and the model revises. The COA is run in a StarCraft II (PySC2) game built as the TigerClaw scenario.
numbers: Per method: 5 COAs x 10 simulations = 50 rollouts. Feedback rounds: none, 1, 2. Baselines: expert human, A3C RL (vector, image), Autocurriculum RL (vector, image). Autocurriculum needed 112 thousand battles, 70 million timesteps. COA-GPT takes seconds; with commander interaction a few minutes.
quote: COA-GPT generates better COAs after receiving feedback from humans, outperforming all baselines
limits: Baseline numbers copied from a prior paper, not rerun. Enemy is the default scripted game AI, not an adaptive opponent. Authors built the system. Human feedback was two fixed scripted sentences, not real commanders.
agent_relevance: Shows generate, simulate, revise works with an LLM generator and a code simulator as judge. Tested against a scripted enemy, so it does not show robustness to enemy moves.

source: Goecks & Waytowich (2024) COA-GPT results on reward and casualties
finding: Without human input, text-only COA-GPT beat all RL baselines on mean total reward. The image variant (COA-GPT-V) matched them. Each feedback round raised mean reward and cut its spread. Friendly casualties stayed higher than the baselines and the human expert; enemy casualties were comparable.
numbers: Reward: +10 per unit crossing a bridge, +10 per enemy killed, -10 per retreat over a crossed bridge, -10 per friendly lost. The human expert had the fewest friendly and most enemy casualties. Exact means are only in figures.
limits: Single scenario. Authors explain the casualties by one-shot commands (no continuous control); a guess, not tested. Reward is a hand-built game score, not a doctrine measure.
agent_relevance: A plan fixed at the start and never revised loses units. Supports a re-plan trigger when real output differs from the plan (G2).

source: Schubert, Hansen, Hoerling, Johansson (2025) Autonomous generation of different courses of action in mechanized combat operations (ICCRTS)
finding: A non-LLM generator for a mechanized battalion. It builds thousands of blue placements, simulates each against the red advance with an event-driven box model, scores outcomes from field-manual loss tables, then clusters similar placements into distinct COAs. Generation and evaluation run in parallel and evaluation steers generation.
numbers: 256 seed configurations from a Nearly Orthogonal Latin Hypercube (16 columns). Search = rank-order selection (best gets weight 256/32896) mixed with a genetic algorithm (5% mutation, 95% crossover), mix weight 0.4 (tested range 0.0 to 0.6). About 4500 groupings for ten platoons. Ten platoons: 456 s expected run time, SD 85 s, 12 CPUs.
limits: Red follows a scripted path from the IFD03 scenario, so this is analysis against one enemy line, not a reacting enemy. Terrain and weather ignored. Loss tables are doctrine-derived, not validated here.
agent_relevance: Closest published design to our S3 and S4: generate many, evaluate by code, cluster to a few distinct options. The clustering step is the 'distinguishable' test done in code.

source: Schubert et al. (2025) design rules: illegal moves and sequential re-planning
finding: A blue unit that would be pulled into combat before reaching its destination is an illegal move and gets a severe penalty; the unit configuration is discarded. As the battle changes, new action alternatives are generated again in sequence.
numbers: Elimination level: a unit below 0.3 of initial relative combat value is removed. 14 boxes on red routes; blue placements drawn from 13 boxes.
limits: Parameters set by the authors, no sensitivity study in the lines read.
agent_relevance: Hard-constraint rejection by code plus re-generation on new state is the same shape as our program-decides loop.

source: Poddar, Esfahani, Dantu, Chowdhury (2025) GenCOA: diverse COAs via binary optimization and graph learning
finding: Splits COA-pool generation into two parts: a genetic algorithm picks diverse task-to-agent allocations, then a graph-attention RL network (CapAM) orders tasks per agent. Pool size 20.
numbers: CapAM mean absolute percent error 4.07% vs the exact TOPTW optimiser, 10 to 100 times faster (solver capped at 180 s). GA takes about 25 min for 20 COAs (2 agents, 100 tasks), up to 50 min with 5 agents. GA raises pool diversity about 10% over random allocation. GenCOA beat the GA-ablated version on 14 of 20 COAs (3 agents) and 13 of 20 (5 agents) at p<0.05.
limits: Not military data; synthetic task graphs. Diversity is in task allocation, not in enemy-facing concept.
agent_relevance: Diversity can be optimised directly as a term in the objective rather than hoped for from sampling.

source: Poddar et al. (2025) GenCOA robustness tests
finding: Under added travel-time noise, the best and worst COAs kept their quartile; the middle ones swapped places. When graph edges were removed at random, at least one COA in the pool stayed valid up to 5% of edges removed.
numbers: Noise levels 5, 10, 15, 20% of edges. Best-ranked COA stayed number 1 until 20% noise, then fell to number 2. Validity test: edges removed up to 5% or more.
limits: Preliminary experiments per the authors. Only travel-time noise, no adversary.
agent_relevance: Evidence that a pool is worth keeping. Close score gaps between options are unstable, so do not trust small differences in a ranking.

source: Vidra & Kanhai (2026) Adversarial Course-of-Action Generation: COA-Bench
finding: Offline synthetic benchmark of COA generation under blue-vs-red self-play. Drawing 8 red responses and keeping the strongest cuts blue's advantage. A council of 5 role-specialised blue proposers with red-team critique and revision gave about the same result.
numbers: 50 synthetic scenarios, 5 templates. Best-of-8 red response: blue advantage .516 to .485, blue win rate .920 to .820. Doctrine-aware selector: .488 and .800. Two-stage council: .509 advantage, .820 win rate. 95% bootstrap intervals over 50 scenarios.
limits: Fully synthetic. Quality score, doctrine rubric and Lanchester-style win check are invented by the authors, who warn they may reward things experts would reject. Looks like an industry report, not peer reviewed.
agent_relevance: The council added no measurable gain over one sampled-and-critiqued policy. Matches our G4 warning on persona voters.

source: Vidra & Kanhai (2026) COA-Bench: a benchmark-design failure found by the authors
finding: Scenario framing was stored as metadata but had no effect on generated COA content. The authors found and fixed it. They also renamed metrics because reusing 'COA matching' and 'COA generation' implied a link to a formal decision function that did not exist.
numbers: Reported as a design issue, no effect size.
limits: Self-reported audit.
agent_relevance: A cheap check for our harness: change the input and confirm the output changes, before trusting any comparison of options.

source: Park, Shim, Kim (2026) Architecture of an AI-based automated COA generation system for military operations
finding: A design paper, not an experiment. It maps doctrine steps (intelligence preparation of the battlefield, friendly COA development, enemy COA analysis, wargaming, comparison) onto software modules. For enemy COA analysis it says to form several enemy COAs, compare, rank, and pick the most likely.
numbers: No measured results. Three-phase doctrinal templating of the enemy plus an integrated architecture figure.
limits: No data. The authors say fielded systems are hard to assess because of secrecy.
agent_relevance: Confirms that modelling the opponent's options is its own stage, separate from generating friendly COAs.

source: Rivera, Mukobi, Reuel, Lamparth, Smith, Schneider (2024) Escalation Risks from Language Models in Military and Diplomatic Decision-Making
finding: Eight LLM nation agents played a turn-based wargame (27 actions each turn) in three scenarios. All five models (GPT-4, GPT-3.5, Claude 2, Llama-2-70B-Chat, GPT-4-Base) escalated at first and none de-escalated significantly. Sudden jumps were hard to predict.
numbers: GPT-3.5, neutral scenario: escalation score 10.15 to 26.02 (+256%). 14 turns per run. GPT-4-Base (no RLHF) was the most unpredictable.
limits: Agents choose from a fixed action menu, not free-form COAs. World model was GPT-3.5. Results depend on prompt and nation text; appendix tests show prompt sensitivity.
agent_relevance: A model playing the adversary drifts toward escalation. In S4, do not trust model-played enemy replies without a code rule.

source: Rivera et al. (2024) qualitative reasons the models gave
finding: The abstract reports arms-race dynamics, nuclear use in rare cases, and justifications based on deterrence and first-strike logic.
numbers: No count of nuclear cases read in the lines opened.
limits: Abstract-level statement; full-text counts not captured.
agent_relevance: Stated reasons for an action can sound sound while the action is poor. Supports G2: judge by outcome, not by the written reason.

source: Lamparth, Corso, Ganz, Mastro, Schneider, Trinkunas (2024) Human vs. Machine: wargame simulations
finding: 214 national security experts in 48 teams played a US-China crisis wargame; LLMs (GPT-3.5, GPT-4, GPT-4o) simulated teams on the same scenario. The overall action mix overlapped strongly with humans, but model teams differed systematically in strategy preferences.
numbers: N = 214 humans, 48 teams. Four randomised move-one treatments (AI accuracy high/low x crew training high/low). Move two: escalating or status-quo adversary. Bootstrap 95% intervals.
limits: Humans chose from a fixed response set. Only three OpenAI models.
agent_relevance: Model role-play has the right shape but wrong tendencies. Treat simulated enemy replies as hypotheses.

source: Lamparth et al. (2024) sensitivity findings
finding: LLM teams reacted to instructions in the prompt (GPT-3.5 chose 'Fire at Chinese vessels' more often under some), showed no sensitivity to player background, and held 'farcical' discussions. In move two there was no significant difference across LLMs.
numbers: Three models compared with the human group.
limits: Qualitative judgement by the authors.
agent_relevance: Prompt wording moves model behaviour more than the simulated person's profile does. Persona prompts are weak levers.

source: Shrivastava, Lamparth, Hullman (2024) Measuring free-form decision-making inconsistency of LMs in military crisis simulations
finding: A BERTScore-based inconsistency score on free-form crisis recommendations. All five LMs gave recommendations that differ in meaning across repeated samples, even with country names anonymised.
numbers: Models: Claude 3.5 Sonnet, GPT-3.5 Turbo, GPT-4, GPT-4o, GPT-4o mini. 20 simulations per distribution, temperature 1.0. Score 0 = identical, near 1 = unrelated; one GPT-4 pair scored 0.73, the maximum seen. Claude 3.5 Sonnet and GPT-4o mini were least inconsistent.
limits: Metric validated on TruthfulQA text pairs, not on COAs rated by experts. A low score means agreement, not correctness.
agent_relevance: Candidates from one prompt really do differ in substance, so sampling gives concept diversity. The metric is a code-side distinctness check.

source: Shrivastava et al. (2024) what lowers inconsistency
finding: Adding a concrete incident (a continuation) lowered inconsistency for most models. The authors guess this is because the decision space gets smaller. Country anonymisation did not change inconsistency for most models.
numbers: Two continuations tested: status quo and revisionist counterpart.
limits: Explanation is a hypothesis. Temperature ablation numbers were not captured.
agent_relevance: A narrower, better specified problem gives more agreeing plans. Restating the situation as concrete facts before generating COAs should reduce wasted spread.

source: Matlin et al. (2026) Shall We Play a Game? Language Models for Open-ended Wargames
finding: Scoping review of 223 AI-in-wargames papers (to 1 May 2026) coded by whether the LM controls player actions, adjudication, or both.
numbers: Only 20 of 223 studies (9%) give the LM both roles.
limits: Coverage review, not an outcome review. It does not rate whether wargames improved plans.
agent_relevance: The open question is adjudication: who decides what an action causes. In our loop, code or a simulator should adjudicate where it can.

source: Hogan & Brennen (2024) Open-Ended Wargames with Large Language Models (Snow Globe)
finding: Snow Globe is a multi-agent LLM system with control, player and observer agents that plays text-based qualitative wargames. The control agent adjudicates each round. The game can be replayed many times to see a range of outcomes.
numbers: No quantitative comparison with humans in the text read.
limits: System description and demo. LLM adjudication accuracy untested in the text read.
agent_relevance: A template for testing one plan against many sampled enemy replies. Ground adjudication in rules where possible.

source: Yin et al. (2025) WGSR-Bench: wargame-based strategic reasoning benchmark
finding: Splits strategic reasoning into situational awareness, opponent modelling and strategy generation. Humans beat all tested models on situational awareness and on opponent modelling.
numbers: Situational awareness: humans 79.9, best AI (Doubao-v1) 58.2, gap 21.7. Complex situation analysis: humans 85.9%, best multimodal model (GLM-4V) 37.5%, gap 48.4 points. Opponent modelling: untrained general humans 77.9, above every LLM tested.
limits: Models are early 2025. Gaps may have narrowed. Human sample size not captured.
agent_relevance: The weak spots are reading the situation and the opponent, the inputs to COA analysis. Supply them as structured facts and check them with code.

source: Klein, Calderwood, Clinton-Cirocco (1986) Rapid decision making on the fire ground
finding: Founding study of recognition-primed decision making: experienced fireground commanders mostly did not compare options. They recognised the situation, imagined one workable option, and acted if it passed.
numbers: From memory, not verified this session: about 26 commanders, about 156 decisions, roughly 80% single-option. Check before citing.
limits: Crossref confirmed the paper exists. Text not opened (DTIC and publisher returned 403). Fireground, not staff planning with time.
agent_relevance: The standing challenge to the doctrine rule 'compare several COAs'. Supports G1: add alternatives only on a failing signal.

source: Thunholm (2004) Planning under time pressure: an attempt toward a prescriptive model of military tactical decision making
finding: Work on a shortened planning process for tactical staffs under time pressure, in the RPD tradition.
numbers: No numbers verified. Crossref confirmed DOI 10.1201/b12472-6.
limits: Not opened. Do not cite results until read.
agent_relevance: Candidate source on whether one good plan plus a test beats several plans under time limits.

source: Pounds & Fallesen (1998) Problem solving of mid-career Army officers: identifying natural reasoning (ARI)
finding: US Army Research Institute work on how officers actually reason on tactical problems. Related: Fallesen & Pounds (1996) Reasoning patterns in tactical problem solving; Pounds & Fallesen (1995) Familiarity effects on strategy use.
numbers: No numbers verified. Crossref confirmed titles and years only.
limits: Not opened (DTIC 403).
agent_relevance: Likely the best empirical source on how many options real staff officers generate and compare. Priority read for angle B.

source: Access limits in this pass
finding: WebSearch quota ran out after one call. Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex rate-limited. DTIC, ArmyUpress, ScienceDirect, JCS and ResearchGate returned 403. The 2022 FM 5-0 and JP 5-0 were not opened.
numbers: 12 documents were opened (3 lines from the Army article, the rest arXiv papers).
limits: 'No controlled single-vs-multi COA study found' means none in opened sources only.
agent_relevance: The human-experiment half of the subfield (Klein, Thunholm, Fallesen, Army Research Institute) is a gap for the next pass.
